questions.q: Which of these sentences describes the weather and not the climate?
o: It is raining heavily in Shillong this afternoon.
Shillong has had cool summers year after year for many decades.
India receives most of its rainfall during a specific period of the year.
The pattern of seasons in a region is closely connected with its climate.
questions.a: 'It is raining heavily in Shillong this afternoon' describes the weather, because weather is what we experience in a particular hour or day.

questions.q: In the traditional division of the year into six ritus, which ritu is the rainy season?
o: Varsha
Sharad
Hemanta
Grishma
questions.a: Varsha is the rainy season among the six ritus.

questions.q:
Match each ritu in Column A with its meaning in Column B.
Column A: 1. Vasanta  2. Grishma  3. Hemanta  4. Shishir
Column B: a. pre-winter  b. winter  c. spring  d. summer
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b: vasanta is spring, grishma is summer, hemanta is pre-winter and shishir is winter.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A list of India's seasons usually has at least one more season than the four main seasons found across most regions of the world.
Reason (R): Seasons occur as the Earth revolves around the Sun.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: seasons everywhere come from the Earth's revolution, but India's extra season is there because it receives rainfall during a specific period of the year, the rainy season or monsoon.

questions.q: (a) What is climate, according to the chapter? (b) Write one sentence about your own town that describes its climate rather than its weather.
questions.a: (a) Climate is the pattern of weather an area or region experiences over a long period of time, several decades at least. (b) Any sentence about a long-term pattern, for example: 'For as long as records exist, our town has had very hot summers and a rainy season from June to September.'
s: (a) Defines climate as the pattern of weather of a region over a long period (several decades at least)
(b) Gives a sentence describing a long-term pattern, not one day's or one hour's weather

questions.q: True or False? 'Seasons occur as the Earth revolves around the Sun, and each season recurs every year.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says seasons occur as the Earth revolves around the Sun; each season lasts a few months and recurs every year in a cycle.
s: States the verdict: True
Explains that seasons come from the Earth's revolution around the Sun, each lasting a few months and recurring every year

questions.q: Answer in one line each, using the chapter's recap. (a) What is weather? (b) What happens to seasons every year? (c) What is climate?
questions.a: (a) Weather is what we experience from day to day: windy, rainy, hot, dry and so on. (b) Seasons recur every year, and the weather of a place is different in every season. (c) Climate is the long-term pattern of weather in a particular region.
s: (a) Weather: what we experience from day to day
(b) Seasons recur every year, with different weather in each
(c) Climate: the long-term pattern in a particular region

questions.q:
Rohan writes in his travel report: 'Our holiday town has a rainy climate, because it rained on all seven days we stayed there last July.'
(a) Is Rohan describing the town's weather or its climate? Give the reason using the chapter's time scale.
(b) Explain why one rainy week in July cannot show the town's climate, using the idea of seasons.
(c) Rewrite his sentence so that it correctly describes the town's climate.
questions.a: (a) Weather: rain over seven days is what is experienced from hour to hour and day to day; climate is the pattern over several decades at least. (b) July falls in the monsoon or rainy season, which recurs every year, and the weather changes with the season; one rainy week in that season says nothing about the other seasons or about the pattern over decades. (c) For example: 'Weather records of the town over the last thirty years or more show heavy rain in the monsoon months every year.' Any sentence describing a pattern over several decades is accepted.
s: (a) Weather, because it covers days, not several decades
(b) July is in the rainy season; one week of one season is not the long-term pattern
(c) A sentence stating a pattern over several decades

questions.q:
Using the six traditional ritus of the chapter (vasanta, grishma, varsha, sharad, hemanta, shishir), name the ritu in which each of these most likely happens.
(a) The first heavy rains of the year fill the rivers and soak the fields.
(b) The hottest, driest weeks of the year arrive.
(c) In some places trees shed their leaves or change colour in the ritu that comes straight after the rainy season.
(d) Some animals have grown thick fur in the coldest months.
(e) Trees and shrubs burst into bloom at the onset of the ritu that comes just before grishma.
questions.a: (a) Varsha (rainy season). (b) Grishma (summer). (c) Sharad (autumn). (d) Shishir (winter). (e) Vasanta (spring).
s: (a) Varsha
(b) Grishma
(c) Sharad
(d) Shishir
(e) Vasanta

questions.q: In which climate region of India is most of the country's wheat grown?
o: The subtropical northern plains
The tropical wet western coastal strip
The semi-arid central Deccan Plateau
The arid Thar Desert
questions.a: Most of India's wheat is grown in the northern plains, which have a subtropical climate.

questions.q: A farmer moves from a region with hot summers, mild winters and moderate rainfall in the rainy season to a region with extremely hot days, cool nights and very little rainfall. Which change in his way of farming will matter most?
o: He must find ways to collect and save water.
He must protect his crops from cold, snowy winters.
He must drain away the extra water of very heavy monsoon rain.
He must switch to rice and spices, which suit his new region.
questions.a: He has moved from the semi-arid Deccan Plateau to the arid Thar, where there is very little rainfall, so he must find ways to collect and save water, as people there have had to do.

questions.q:
Match each region in Column A with its climate in Column B.
Column A: 1. The Thar Desert  2. The central Deccan Plateau  3. The western coastal strip  4. The northern plains
Column B: a. semi-arid  b. tropical wet  c. arid  d. subtropical
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-b, 4-d: the Thar is arid, the central Deccan Plateau semi-arid, the western coastal strip tropical wet and the northern plains subtropical.

questions.q:
Read the statements about India's climates.
I. In a temperate climate the winters are moderately cold and the summers not too hot.
II. The tropical wet climate of the western coastal strip favours the growing of rice and spices.
III. The central Deccan Plateau has extremely hot days, cool nights and very little rainfall.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
o: I and II only
II and III only
I and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: Statements I and II are correct. Statement III describes the arid Thar; the Deccan Plateau is semi-arid, with hot summers, mild winters and moderate rainfall.

questions.q: (a) Name the climate of the Himalayan mountains in the north. (b) Give its two features stated in the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Alpine. (b) Cold, snowy winters and cool summers.
s: (a) Names the alpine climate
(b) Gives cold, snowy winters and cool summers

questions.q: A cooperative wants to start a farm for rice and spices. Its survey describes two possible regions without naming them. Region X has hot summers, mild winters and moderate rainfall during the rainy season. Region Y receives heavy rainfall during the monsoon months. (a) Which region suits rice and spices better? Name its climate type. (b) Name the climate type of the other region and say why it suits these crops less.
questions.a: (a) Region Y: heavy monsoon rainfall gives the tropical wet climate of the western coastal strip, which the chapter calls favourable to the growing of rice and spices. (b) Region X has the semi-arid climate of the central Deccan Plateau; it gets only moderate rainfall, not the heavy rainfall that makes the tropical wet climate favourable to rice and spices.
s: (a) Region Y, tropical wet climate, favourable to rice and spices
(b) Region X is semi-arid with only moderate rainfall, so it suits them less

questions.q: Give one feature, from the chapter, of each of these climates: (a) the arid climate of the Thar Desert; (b) the semi-arid climate of the central Deccan Plateau; (c) the tropical climate of eastern India and the southern peninsula.
questions.a: (a) Extremely hot days, cool nights and very little rainfall. (b) Hot summers, mild winters and moderate rainfall during the rainy season. (c) A mild winter and distinct wet and dry periods controlled by monsoon winds.
s: (a) One correct feature of the arid Thar climate
(b) One correct feature of the semi-arid Deccan climate
(c) One correct feature of the tropical climate of the east and south

questions.q:
A home-goods company has four shops. Shop A is in a village high in the Himalayas, Shop B in a hill station lower in the Himalayas, Shop C in a town of the northern plains and Shop D in a town on the western coastal strip. Last year's sales (invented figures) were: room heaters, A 900, B 300, C 250, D 10; gumboots for wading through rainwater, A 40, B 120, C 90, D 700.
(a) Which shop sold the most gumboots? Name its climate and the reason.
(b) Shop C sells room heaters in one part of the year and cooling fans in another. Which feature of its climate explains this?
(c) Why did Shop A sell so many more room heaters than Shop D? Name both climates.
(d) The company has 400 extra room heaters for Shops A and B only. The manager says, 'Send 200 to each, because both are in the Himalayas.' Use last year's heater sales and the chapter to judge this and suggest a better split.
questions.a: (a) Shop D (700 pairs): the tropical wet climate, because the western coastal strip receives heavy rainfall during the monsoon months. (b) The subtropical climate of the northern plains has very hot summers and cold winters. (c) Shop A has the alpine climate with cold, snowy winters; Shop D has the tropical wet climate, which has no such cold winter in the chapter's description, so it sold only 10. (d) The equal split is not sensible: Shop A is high in the Himalayas (alpine, cold snowy winters) while Shop B is lower down (temperate, only moderately cold winters), and A sold 900 heaters against B's 300, three times as many. Splitting 400 in the ratio 900 : 300 = 3 : 1 gives 300 to Shop A and 100 to Shop B.
s: (a) Shop D, tropical wet climate from heavy monsoon rain
(b) Subtropical: very hot summers and cold winters
(c) A alpine with cold snowy winters against D tropical wet
(d) Rejects the equal split (alpine vs temperate, 900 vs 300) and proposes 300 to A, 100 to B

questions.q:
A visitor writes in a blog: 'India is a hot, tropical country, so its climate is hot and wet everywhere.' Evaluate this claim using the chapter.
(a) Give evidence from the Himalayan mountains.
(b) Give evidence from the Thar Desert.
(c) Give evidence from the northern plains.
(d) Give evidence from one more region of your choice.
(e) Give your verdict and say what mistake the visitor has made.
questions.a: (a) The Himalayan mountains have an alpine climate with cold, snowy winters and cool summers, not hot. (b) The Thar has an arid climate with very little rainfall and cool nights, not wet. (c) The northern plains are subtropical, with very hot summers but cold winters. (d) For example, the central Deccan Plateau is semi-arid, with mild winters and only moderate rainfall; or the lower Himalayas and hilly areas are temperate, with summers not too hot. (e) The claim is wrong: India is a land of diversity in climate. The visitor has taken one type, the tropical wet climate of the western coastal strip (heavy monsoon rain), and applied it to the whole country.
s: (a) Alpine Himalayas: cold, snowy winters and cool summers
(b) Arid Thar: very little rainfall, cool nights
(c) Subtropical northern plains: cold winters as well as very hot summers
(d) One more correct contrasting region and its climate
(e) Verdict that the claim is wrong; one region's tropical wet climate is not the whole of India's diverse climate

questions.q: Why are places near the Equator warmer than places near the poles?
o: At the Equator the sun's rays are nearly perpendicular, so their energy is focused on a smaller area.
Places at the Equator are much closer to the Sun than the poles are.
At the Equator the sun's rays pass through more of the atmosphere.
At the Equator the sun's rays are oblique and spread over a larger area.
questions.a: At the Equator the sun's rays are nearly perpendicular, so their energy is focused on a smaller area of the Earth's surface; near the poles the rays are oblique and spread out.

questions.q: Which of these observations can NOT be explained by latitude alone?
o: Nagpur's summers are much hotter than Mumbai's, although the two lie at a similar latitude.
Kanniyakumari is warm almost all year, while Srinagar is much cooler.
The Nicobar Islands, close to the Equator, are warm or hot almost throughout the year.
The polar regions receive less heat than the equatorial zone.
questions.a: Nagpur and Mumbai lie at a similar latitude, so latitude cannot explain their difference; it comes from proximity to the sea, which moderates Mumbai's temperature.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Many peaks of the Himalayas stay covered in snow.
Reason (R): The Himalayas are so high that many peaks keep a temperature below water's freezing point.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the peaks are so high that their temperature stays below freezing, so the snow does not melt.

questions.q: A class wants to test how altitude alone affects temperature. Which pair of places should it compare?
o: Two places at the same latitude and the same distance from the sea, but at very different heights
Two coastal towns at the same height but at very different latitudes
A coastal town and an inland town at the same latitude and the same height
Two places at different latitudes, different heights and different distances from the sea
questions.a: Two places at the same latitude and the same distance from the sea but at different heights, so that only altitude differs and the other factors cannot explain the difference.

questions.q: Give the two reasons the chapter gives for why the temperature decreases as the altitude increases.
questions.a: (1) The atmospheric pressure, and so the air density, decreases with altitude, and as air gets less dense it gets cooler. (2) The sun heats the Earth's surface, so the farther the air is from the surface, the less hot it is.
s: Air pressure and density fall with height, and thinner air is cooler
The sun heats the surface, so air farther from the surface is less hot

questions.q: True or False? 'The polar regions are colder because the sun's rays there pass through less of the Earth's atmosphere.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Near the poles the rays are oblique, so their energy is spread over a larger surface, and they pass through more of the atmosphere, which further dissipates their energy.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: the oblique rays spread over a larger area and pass through more of the atmosphere

questions.q: The range of temperature is the difference between the maximum and the minimum. Town K has a summer high of 36 degrees C and a winter low of 15 degrees C (invented figures). (a) Find Town K's range. (b) Town L, at the same latitude, has a range of only 12 degrees C. Which town is more likely to be on the coast? (c) Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) 36 - 15 = 21 degrees C. (b) Town L. (c) The sea acts as a moderator of temperature, so coastal places have summers that are not too hot and winters that are not too cold, giving a smaller range.
s: (a) Range of Town K = 21 degrees C
(b) Town L is more likely on the coast
(c) The sea moderates temperature, so the coastal range is smaller

questions.q:
The chapter gives these figures: Mumbai, summers around 32 degrees C and winters around 18 degrees C; Nagpur, up to 44 degrees C in summer and about 10 degrees C in winter. Both lie at a similar latitude.
(a) Work out the range of temperature of each city.
(b) By how many degrees is Nagpur's range greater than Mumbai's?
(c) Why can latitude not explain this difference?
(d) Explain why Nagpur's summers are hotter AND its winters colder than Mumbai's.
questions.a: (a) Mumbai: 32 - 18 = 14 degrees C. Nagpur: 44 - 10 = 34 degrees C. (b) 34 - 14 = 20 degrees C. (c) The two cities lie at a similar latitude, so the sun's rays reach them at much the same angle; latitude affects both alike. (d) Mumbai is near the sea, which acts as a moderator: it keeps summers from getting too hot and winters from getting too cold. Nagpur is far from the coast, and inland temperatures are more extreme, with higher summer and lower winter temperatures.
s: (a) Ranges: Mumbai 14 and Nagpur 34 degrees C
(b) Nagpur's range is greater by 20 degrees C
(c) Similar latitude means latitude affects both alike
(d) Sea moderates Mumbai; inland Nagpur has more extreme summers and winters

questions.q:
Kabir says: 'The Nicobar Islands are close to the Equator, so they must have the largest range of temperature in India, because the hottest places have the biggest difference between summer and winter.'
(a) Using latitude, describe the Nicobar Islands' temperature through the year.
(b) Using the islands' position in the sea, describe their range of temperature.
(c) Explain the difference between a place being hot and a place having a large range of temperature.
(d) Two invented towns lie at about the same latitude: coastal Town S has summers of about 31 degrees C and winters of about 22 degrees C; inland Town T has summers of about 44 degrees C and winters of about 8 degrees C. Work out both ranges and say which kind of place has the larger range.
(e) Give your verdict on Kabir's claim.
questions.a: (a) Being close to the Equator, the islands get nearly perpendicular sun rays and are warm or hot almost throughout the year. (b) Surrounded by sea, which moderates temperature, their summers are not too hot and winters not too cold, so the range is small. (c) Being hot is about how high the temperature is; the range is the difference between the maximum and the minimum, so a place can be hot all year with a small range. (d) Town S: 31 - 22 = 9 degrees C; Town T: 44 - 8 = 36 degrees C, four times as large: places far from the sea have the larger range. (e) Kabir is wrong: the Nicobar Islands should have a small range, and the largest ranges are found far inland.
s: (a) Near the Equator: warm or hot almost all year
(b) The sea moderates temperature, so the range is small
(c) Distinguishes being hot from having a large range (max minus min)
(d) Ranges 9 and 36 degrees C: inland places have larger ranges
(e) Verdict: the claim is wrong

questions.q: What does the word 'topography' mean in the chapter?
o: The totality of the physical surface features of an area, such as mountains, valleys, slopes and coasts
The pattern of weather of a region over three decades or more
The direction and speed of the winds over an area
The amount of rain or snow a region receives in a year
questions.a: Topography is the totality of the physical surface features of an area, such as mountains, hills, valleys, slopes and coasts.

questions.q: In summer, winds blowing from the west into Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh bring dry, hot air and severe heat waves. Why are these winds dry and hot?
o: They have travelled over the deserts of Arabia to Afghanistan.
They have crossed the Bay of Bengal.
They have come down from the snowy Himalayan peaks.
They have blown in from the Indian Ocean.
questions.a: They have travelled over the deserts of Arabia to Afghanistan, so they bring dry, hot air.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): An urban heat island is often much warmer than the region around it.
Reason (R): It has a large number of buildings and other concrete structures and very little vegetation, which trap the heat.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the many concrete structures and little vegetation trap the heat, making the city warmer than its surroundings.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
I. Winds coming from the sea bring moisture over the land, which may result in rainfall.
II. The Himalayas and the Karakoram ranges fully stop every cold wind from reaching the Indian subcontinent.
III. A microclimate can influence the crops grown and the health of the people living there.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: Statements I and III are correct. Statement II is wrong: the ranges protect the subcontinent only to some extent, and in winter cold winds from across the Himalayas still creep into the foothills.

questions.q: (a) What is a microclimate? (b) Give one example of a microclimate from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) A microclimate is a climate localised in a small area, which differs from the climate of the surrounding region. (b) An enclosed valley, some forests, or an urban heat island (a city with many buildings and little vegetation).
s: (a) A climate localised in a small area, different from the surrounding region
(b) One correct example: an enclosed valley, a forest or an urban heat island

questions.q: Ritu wants to describe the climate of her district for a project. She has noted only the daily temperature for the last 5 years. Using what the chapter says a description of climate must include, name (a) two kinds of record she is missing and (b) how long her records should cover.
questions.a: (a) Precipitation (rain or snowfall, fog or mist) and wind conditions. (b) Three decades or more; 5 years is far too short.
s: (a) Names precipitation and wind conditions as missing
(b) States the records should cover three decades or more

questions.q:
A weather diary (invented figures) shows two events. In a May week, a town in Rajasthan, whose usual afternoon high is 41 degrees C, reached 47 degrees C. In a January week, a town in the Himalayan foothills, whose usual night low is 6 degrees C, fell to 0 degrees C. Kiran says, 'Both events happened because of the towns' latitude.'
(a) By how many degrees did each town move away from its usual reading, and in which direction?
(b) Name the cause the chapter gives for each event.
(c) Judge Kiran's claim, using both the data and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Rajasthan: 47 - 41 = 6 degrees hotter than usual. Foothills: 6 - 0 = 6 degrees colder than usual. (b) The heat wave: winds from the west that have travelled over the deserts of Arabia to Afghanistan bring dry, hot air. The cold wave: cold winds from across the Himalayas creep into the foothills. (c) Kiran is wrong: a town's latitude does not change from one week to the next, so it cannot explain a sudden 6-degree jump either way. Both events show the factor of winds, which move masses of warmer or cooler air from one region to another.
s: (a) 6 degrees hotter in Rajasthan, 6 degrees colder in the foothills
(b) Dry hot westerly winds; cold winds from across the Himalayas
(c) Rejects the claim: latitude is fixed, so winds moving warm or cold air explain the sudden changes

questions.q:
The chapter names five factors that determine the climate: latitude, altitude, proximity to the sea, winds and topography. Name the factor at work in each case.
(a) The Himalayas and the Karakoram protect, to some extent, the Indian subcontinent from the cold winds of Central Asia.
(b) Shimla is cooler than the plains below it.
(c) Hot, dry air from the deserts of Arabia reaches Punjab in summer.
(d) Kanniyakumari is warm almost throughout the year.
(e) A town on the coast has summers that are not too hot and winters that are not too cold.
questions.a: (a) Topography. (b) Altitude. (c) Winds. (d) Latitude. (e) Proximity to the sea.
s: (a) Topography
(b) Altitude
(c) Winds
(d) Latitude
(e) Proximity to the sea

questions.q: The word 'monsoon' comes from the Arabic word mausim. What does mausim mean?
o: Season
Rain
Wind
Ocean
questions.a: Mausim means 'season'.

questions.q: Mawsynram in Meghalaya receives about 11,000 mm of rain a year. How many metres of rain is this? (1 m = 1,000 mm)
questions.a: 11,000 mm divided by 1,000 is 11 m.

questions.q: A weather log for a town on the west coast of south India reads (invented): late May, hot and dry; 3 June, winds from the southwest and the first heavy rain; June to September, heavy rain on most days. Which conclusion agrees with the chapter?
o: The June to September rain is the summer or southwest monsoon, which advances from the southern tip of India in early June, so the town gets it early.
The rain began on 3 June because by then the monsoon had covered the entire subcontinent.
The word 'southwest' tells us the winds were blowing towards the southwest.
The rain came because the land was cooler than the ocean in late May.
questions.a: The June to September rain is the summer or southwest monsoon: it advances from the southern tip of India in early June, and 'southwest' is the direction the winds come from.

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with Column B.
Column A: 1. The Asian landmass in summer  2. The Asian landmass in winter  3. The western slopes of the Western Ghats in the southwest monsoon  4. The Deccan Plateau east of the Ghats in the southwest monsoon
Column B: a. high pressure  b. low pressure  c. much rainfall  d. less rainfall, often with interruptions
questions.a: 1-b, 2-a, 3-c, 4-d: the land heats in summer and has low pressure, cools in winter and has high pressure; the Ghats' western slopes get much rain and the plateau to the east gets less.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the southwest monsoon, the western slopes of the Western Ghats receive much rainfall.
Reason (R): Mawsynram in Meghalaya receives the highest average annual rainfall in the world.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the Ghats get much rain because they act as a barrier to the monsoon winds, which has nothing to do with Mawsynram's rainfall.

questions.q: Air always flows from high pressure to low pressure. Using this rule, state the direction in which the monsoon winds blow (a) in summer and (b) in winter.
questions.a: (a) In summer, from the cooler, high-pressure ocean towards the hot, low-pressure land. (b) In winter, from the cooler, high-pressure land towards the warmer, lower-pressure ocean.
s: (a) Summer: from ocean to land
(b) Winter: from land to ocean

questions.q: Explain in three steps how the summer monsoon brings rain to India. (a) What happens to the Asian landmass as summer begins? (b) In which direction are the winds drawn, and why? (c) Why does rain fall?
questions.a: (a) The Asian landmass heats up faster than the ocean, creating a powerful low-pressure system over it. (b) Winds are drawn from the cooler, high-pressure ocean towards the hot land, because air flows from high to low pressure. (c) These ocean winds carry moisture that condenses over the warmer land and falls as heavy monsoon rain.
s: (a) The land heats up and forms a low-pressure system
(b) Winds drawn from the high-pressure ocean to the land, as air flows from high to low pressure
(c) The moisture the winds carry condenses over the land and falls as rain

questions.q:
A school radio show called 'Monsoon Magic' reads out this script: 'During the monsoon months the rivers fill up, the soil is soaked with water, crops grow and life thrives. Mawsynram in Meghalaya gets about 11,000 mm of rain a year, the highest average in the world. The rains have even inspired ragas in Carnatic and Hindustani music, such as Meghamalhar and amruthavarshini.' A student reporter adds that the rain gauge at her school measured 1,100 mm last year.
(a) Name the two ragas mentioned in the script.
(b) Name the state in which the place with the world's highest average rainfall lies.
(c) How many times the rain at the reporter's school does Mawsynram receive?
(d) From the script, give two ways in which the monsoon months bring life.
questions.a: (a) Meghamalhar and amruthavarshini. (b) Meghalaya. (c) 11,000 / 1,100 = 10 times. (d) Any two: the rivers fill up; the soil is soaked with water; crops grow.
s: (a) Names Meghamalhar and amruthavarshini
(b) Meghalaya
(c) 10 times
(d) Two of: rivers fill up, soil soaked, crops grow

questions.q:
A water board compares rainfall records (invented figures, mm) for three towns of south India over three parts of the year: January to May, June to September and October to December. Town P, on the western slopes of the Western Ghats: 150, 3,400, 250. Town Q, on the east coast: 100, 350, 750. Town R, on the Deccan Plateau: 60, 520, 120.
(a) Find each town's yearly total and the percentage of it that falls in October to December.
(b) Name the monsoon that brings Town Q its October to December rain, and explain how it can bring rain although its winds are dry.
(c) From which direction do the winds that bring Town Q's main rain come? Give the reason from the name of the monsoon.
(d) A guidebook says, 'Every town in south India gets most of its rain from the southwest monsoon.' Test this claim against all three towns.
(e) In which town would a failure of the winter monsoon cut the yearly rain the most? Show the figure.
questions.a: (a) P: 150 + 3,400 + 250 = 3,800 mm, 250/3,800 = about 6.6%. Q: 1,200 mm, 750/1,200 = 62.5%. R: 700 mm, 120/700 = about 17.1%. (b) The winter or northeast monsoon. In winter the land cools faster than the ocean, so the winds blow from the land to the ocean and are dry, but a part of them passes over the Bay of Bengal, collects some moisture and brings rain to parts of east and south India. (c) From the northeast: the monsoon is named after the direction its winds come from, as 'southwest' is for the summer monsoon. (d) The claim fails: it holds for P (3,400/3,800, about 89.5%) and R (520/700, about 74.3%), but Town Q gets only 350/1,200, about 29.2%, from the southwest monsoon. (e) Town Q: it would lose 750 of its 1,200 mm, 62.5% of its yearly rain, far more than P (about 6.6%) or R (about 17.1%).
s: (b) Winter or northeast monsoon: dry land-to-ocean winds pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal
(c) From the northeast, as the name gives the direction the winds come from
(d) Claim fails: true for P and R, but Q gets only about 29.2% from the southwest monsoon
(e) Town Q, 62.5% of its rain

questions.q: Which body keeps track of coming cyclones and gives information on their formation, evolution and place of landing?
o: The India Meteorological Department (IMD)
The National Disaster Response Force (NDRF)
The village panchayat
The state forest department
questions.a: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) tracks coming cyclones.

questions.q: What is a glacial burst?
o: Water of a glacial lake breaking through its barrier of rocks and ice
A glacier sliding down into the plains in summer
A river in the plains overflowing after heavy rain
Sea water flooding a coastal city during a cyclone
questions.a: A glacial burst is when the water of a glacial lake breaks through its barrier of rocks and ice, because glaciers melt too fast or there is too much rain.

questions.q: A class makes a chart of festivals from the chapter's pictures, such as Pongal, Bihu, Onam, Baisakhi and Lohri. Which idea from the chapter best explains why so many Indian festivals exist in rhythm with the year?
o: Our lives are connected with the climate, and India has many festivals associated with seasons and agricultural activities
Festivals are fixed by the weather of the week, so their dates change every year with the forecast
Festivals are held only during the monsoon, when the rivers fill up
Festivals depend on a region's latitude, so they are celebrated only in north India
questions.a: The chapter says the impact of climate is visible in local cultures: India has many festivals associated with seasons and agricultural activities.

questions.q:
Read the statements about climate-related disasters in India.
I. Every year the Indian coastline, especially the eastern coast, witnesses several cyclones.
II. Floods in the Himalayan regions happen only when rivers in the plains burst their banks.
III. In hilly regions the chances of landslides have increased because of human activities such as cutting down forests.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: Statements I and III are correct. Statement II is wrong: in the Himalayan regions floods occur when glacial lakes overflow or burst through their barriers.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Many cities experience flooding when there is heavy rainfall.
Reason (R): Urban surfaces of concrete or asphalt allow rain water to soak quickly into the earth.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: concrete and asphalt do NOT allow water to be absorbed by the earth, which is one reason cities flood.

questions.q: (a) What is a landslide? (b) Name one natural trigger of a landslide given in the chapter.
questions.a: (a) A landslide is the sudden collapse of rock, soil or debris. (b) Heavy rain, earthquakes or volcanic activity.
s: (a) The sudden collapse of rock, soil or debris
(b) One trigger: heavy rain, an earthquake or volcanic activity

questions.q: True or False? 'The National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) is trained to respond only to natural disasters.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The NDRF is specially trained to respond to natural as well as human-made disasters.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: the NDRF responds to natural as well as human-made disasters

questions.q: A reporter describes a cyclone over the Bay of Bengal but mixes up the order: 'P: the winds rotate inwards and form clouds round a cloudless centre. Q: the pressure near the sea becomes lower than in the surrounding areas. R: air from the surrounding areas moves in from the sea, bringing moisture.' (a) Write P, Q and R in the correct order. (b) Why does the air move in at step R? (c) What is the cloudless centre called?
questions.a: (a) Q, then R, then P. (b) Air from the surrounding areas is drawn into the low-pressure area, because the low pressure is an invitation to the air around it. (c) The eye of the cyclone.
s: (a) Correct order Q, R, P
(b) Air is drawn in towards the low-pressure area
(c) The eye of the cyclone

questions.q:
A forest department in Madhya Pradesh records the forest fires of five summers (invented figures). 2020: 40 fires, 28 from human carelessness. 2021: 25 fires, 15 from human carelessness. 2022 (a drought year): 60 fires, 45 from human carelessness. 2023: 30 fires, 18 from human carelessness. 2024 (a drought year): 45 fires, 31 from human carelessness.
(a) Find the total number of fires and the percentage caused by human carelessness.
(b) Find the average number of fires in the drought years and in the other years.
(c) What do (a) and (b) together show about the causes of forest fires named in the chapter?
(d) Recommend one action for the department and justify it using a consequence of forest fires given in the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Total fires = 40 + 25 + 60 + 30 + 45 = 200; carelessness = 28 + 15 + 45 + 18 + 31 = 137, which is 68.5 percent. (b) Drought years: (60 + 45) / 2 = 52.5 fires; other years: (40 + 25 + 30) / 3 = about 31.7 fires. (c) Both causes the chapter names are at work: human carelessness starts most fires, and dry conditions and droughts make many more fires break out. (d) For example, an awareness and patrol drive against careless burning in drought summers, because fires destroy forests, harm wildlife, spoil the air quality and displace local communities, with environmental and economic costs.
s: (a) 200 fires, 137 from carelessness, 68.5 percent
(b) Drought years 52.5, other years about 31.7
(c) Human carelessness and dry/drought conditions both cause fires
(d) One sensible action justified by a chapter consequence of forest fires

questions.q:
A small cloth-dyeing unit in a town uses 60,000 litres of water a month. In a normal year the town supply gives all of it. In a year of monsoon failure (invented figures) the town supply gives only 24,000 litres a month, and the rest has to be bought by tanker at Rs 1,000 for every 6,000 litres. The unit's canteen also finds that its weekly bill for vegetables has risen from Rs 2,000 to Rs 2,600.
(a) How many tankers does the unit need each month, and what do they cost?
(b) Find the percentage rise in the canteen's vegetable bill. Which word does the chapter use for food becoming costlier like this?
(c) Which link stated in the chapter explains why a dyeing unit is hit by a monsoon failure?
(d) The owner says, 'We are a factory, not a farm, so a monsoon failure is none of our business.' Use two facts from the case to judge this.
questions.a: (a) 60,000 - 24,000 = 36,000 litres to buy; 36,000/6,000 = 6 tankers, costing 6 x Rs 1,000 = Rs 6,000 a month. (b) (2,600 - 2,000)/2,000 x 100 = 30 percent; the chapter calls this inflation (costlier food fuels inflation). (c) Industrial activity often depends on predictable weather and the availability of water. (d) The owner is wrong: the unit now pays Rs 6,000 a month for tanker water because the supply fell short, and its canteen pays 30 percent more for vegetables, so a monsoon failure reaches a factory as well as farms.
s: (a) 6 tankers, Rs 6,000 a month
(b) 30 percent; inflation
(c) Industry depends on predictable weather and the availability of water
(d) Rejects the claim with two facts: tanker cost and costlier vegetables

questions.q: Which of these are fossil fuels, according to the chapter?
o: Coal, petroleum oil and natural gas
Firewood, cow dung and straw
Sunlight, wind and running water
Charcoal, biogas and vegetable oil
questions.a: Coal, petroleum oil and natural gas are fossil fuels, formed from remains of plants and animals buried for millions of years.

questions.q: The chapter speaks of building 'resilience' in communities. What does resilience mean?
o: The capacity to withstand or recover quickly from difficulties
Steps that help slow down global warming
Something that can be maintained over a long period of time
The release of greenhouse gases by industry
questions.a: Resilience is the capacity to withstand or recover quickly from difficulties.

questions.q: Which list contains ONLY causes that, according to the chapter, have largely driven climate change since the 19th century?
o: Burning of fossil fuels, deforestation and excessive or wasteful consumption
Burning of fossil fuels, the natural carbon cycle and deforestation
Natural processes of past millennia, harmful industrial practices and deforestation
Planting trees, boosting renewable energy and improving energy efficiency
questions.a: Since the 19th century climate change has been largely driven by human activities: burning of fossil fuels, deforestation, harmful industrial practices and excessive or wasteful consumption.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The natural greenhouse effect warms the Earth enough to support life.
Reason (R): Carbon dioxide and other gases in the atmosphere trap heat from the Sun.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the gases trap heat from the Sun, which keeps the Earth warm enough for life.

questions.q: (a) What is climate change, according to the chapter? (b) Name one human activity that has largely driven it since the 19th century.
questions.a: (a) Climate change refers to significant, long-term changes in the climate, on the scale of the planet or of a region, involving shifts in temperature, precipitation and weather events. (b) Any one: burning of fossil fuels, deforestation, environmentally harmful industrial practices, or excessive or wasteful consumption.
s: (a) Significant, long-term change in the climate
(b) One correct human cause

questions.q: Say whether each action is a measure of climate mitigation, and give the reason. (a) A factory switches from coal to solar power. (b) A family buys a second car only for short trips it could walk. (c) A village plants trees on bare common land.
questions.a: (a) Yes: it boosts renewable energy and cuts greenhouse gas emissions from burning a fossil fuel. (b) No: it burns more fuel and is the kind of excessive consumption that drives climate change. (c) Yes: planting trees is a mitigation measure named in the chapter.
s: (a) Mitigation: renewable energy, fewer emissions
(b) Not mitigation: more fuel burnt, wasteful consumption
(c) Mitigation: planting trees

questions.q: Your school's eco club asks you to draw up a five-point climate plan for the school. Write five actions, and after each say which cause of climate change it tackles or which mitigation measure from the chapter it belongs to. Each action must be something a school can really do.
questions.a: A sample plan: (1) Switch off fans and lights in empty rooms and replace old ones with efficient ones: improving energy efficiency. (2) Put solar panels on the roof: boosting renewable energy. (3) Plant and look after trees on the campus: planting trees, the opposite of deforestation. (4) Encourage walking, cycling or the school bus instead of private cars: cuts greenhouse gas emissions from burning fossil fuels. (5) Run a 'reduce, reuse, repair' drive against wasted food and paper: promotes sustainable lifestyles and tackles excessive or wasteful consumption.
s: Action 1, realistic and linked to a chapter cause or measure
Action 2, realistic and linked to a chapter cause or measure
Action 3, realistic and linked to a chapter cause or measure
Action 4, realistic and linked to a chapter cause or measure
Action 5, realistic and linked to a chapter cause or measure

questions.q:
An exhibition panel at a coal mine reads: 'The coal here formed from plants that died millions of years ago and were buried deep under layers of soil and rock, where heat and pressure slowly turned them into coal. Our nearby power plant burns 2,000 tonnes of this coal every day.' The state plans to replace one quarter of this coal with solar power.
(a) Is coal a fossil fuel? Explain using the panel.
(b) How many tonnes of coal a day will the plan save?
(c) Name the greenhouse gas the chapter mentions and explain how its release affects the climate.
(d) A visitor says, 'Coal formed naturally, so burning it cannot be a cause of today's climate change.' Use the chapter to judge this.
questions.a: (a) Yes: it formed from remains of plants that died millions of years ago and were buried under soil and rock, where heat and pressure turned them into coal, which is how the chapter defines a fossil fuel. (b) 2,000 / 4 = 500 tonnes a day. (c) Carbon dioxide (CO2); released in huge amounts in a few centuries, it traps extra heat, causing rapid global warming and disrupting climate patterns. (d) The visitor is wrong: coal formed naturally over millions of years, but burning it releases huge amounts of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide in just a few centuries; this sudden increase traps extra heat, and the chapter names the burning of fossil fuels as a main human driver of climate change since the 19th century.
s: (a) Yes, with the fossil-fuel formation from buried remains
(b) 500 tonnes a day
(c) Carbon dioxide traps extra heat, causing rapid global warming
(d) Rejects the claim: natural origin, but burning releases CO2 fast and is a main human driver
